prompt: Match each piece of evidence to its factor.
A login asks for a password and then the answer to "your first pet's name". Is that two-factor authentication?
hint: Count the kinds, not the questions.

choices.text: Yes, if the answer is long enough
choices.why: Length does not change the kind.

choices.text: No, because pets are something you have
choices.why: The answer is remembered, so it is something you know.

choices.text: No: both are something you know
choices.why: Right. A longer login, no stronger in kind.

choices.text: Yes, since two separate secrets are asked
choices.why: Two secrets are the same kind and fall the same way.

prompt: Why does a second factor of a different kind help so much against a password from a breach?
hint: Each kind is lost in a different way.

choices.text: It encrypts the password in the breach
choices.why: It cannot touch somebody else's breached database.

choices.text: The attacker with the password still lacks the other factor
choices.why: Right. A stolen password becomes a failed login.

choices.text: Breached passwords stop working after thirty seconds
choices.why: Codes expire; passwords do not.

choices.text: It makes the password itself longer and harder to guess
choices.why: The password is unchanged.

prompt: "The request comes from Brazil" is what, according to the lesson?
hint: Nobody proves who they are by being somewhere.

choices.text: Proof of identity for anyone inside the country
choices.why: That is trust by location again.

choices.text: A signal
choices.why: Right. It raises or lowers suspicion; it proves nothing.

choices.text: A third factor, called somewhere you are
choices.why: Location is not one of the three factors.

choices.text: Something you have, since you have a location
choices.why: A location is not an object in your possession.

prompt: How many seconds does one TOTP step last in the lesson's codes?

choices.text: The server sent a new code at 13:00:30
choices.why: Nothing is sent; both sides compute.

choices.text: The code was used once and expired
choices.why: It was not used; time moved on.

choices.text: The secret rotates every thirty seconds
choices.why: The secret stays the same for as long as MFA is on.

choices.text: A new 30-second step began, so the counter changed
choices.why: Right. Same step, same code.

prompt: Order the steps that make a TOTP code.
hint: From the clock to the six digits.
items: divide the time since 1970 by 30 seconds
compute an HMAC of that counter with the secret
cut the result to six digits
trap: The HMAC needs the counter as its input, and the cut needs the HMAC's output.

prompt: The phone has no connection to the server. How do the two agree on the same code?

choices.text: The codes come from a printed list both keep
choices.why: That describes recovery codes, not TOTP.

choices.text: The phone sends the code to the server in the background
choices.why: There is no connection.

choices.text: Both hold the same secret and the same clock
choices.why: Right. The same inputs give the same output.

choices.text: The server reads the phone's screen
choices.why: It reads what the person types.

prompt: The code 593771 was checked at 13:02:00 and refused. Why?

choices.text: The server expected the code of a later step
choices.why: Right. Four steps had passed.

choices.text: Codes are single-use and it was already used
choices.why: The refusal is about the step, not about use.

choices.text: The secret on the server was different
choices.why: The same code was accepted at 13:00:00.

choices.text: oathtool refuses codes after noon
choices.why: No such rule.

prompt: Why does a server accept a window of one step and no more?
hint: Two costs pull against each other.

choices.text: RFC 6238 forbids any window larger than one step, in every case
choices.why: The lesson gives the trade-off, not a prohibition.

choices.text: A wider window makes codes longer
choices.why: Code length is set separately.

choices.text: Because the phone's clock is always exact
choices.why: If it were, no window would be needed.

choices.text: Small drift only; a wider window lets stolen codes live
choices.why: Right. Tolerance for people, not for attackers.

prompt: The RFC's known secret, time and expected code, used to check an implementation, are called test ___.
Somebody steals the server's database of TOTP secrets. What can they do?

choices.text: Nothing, since the codes change every thirty seconds
choices.why: With the secret, every future code is computable.

choices.text: Read the users' passwords from the secrets
choices.why: TOTP secrets are not passwords.

choices.text: Compute every user's codes, now and later
choices.why: Right. Which is why they are stored encrypted and guarded.

choices.text: Only the codes of the current step
choices.why: Any step is computable from the secret.

prompt: Match each second factor to how it is defeated.

pairs.right: the carrier moves the number to the attacker's SIM
request after request until the victim taps yes
a fake login page asks for it and uses it at once

right_distractors: nothing usable reaches a fake page

prompt: Why does a security key resist a phishing page that TOTP does not?
hint: What does the browser include in what is signed?

choices.text: Security keys only work on the office network
choices.why: They work anywhere; location is not the reason.

choices.text: Phishing pages cannot be opened on a computer with a USB key
choices.why: They open; they just get nothing useful.

choices.text: The signature names the real site's address
choices.why: Right. Nothing to type into the wrong place.

choices.text: Security keys use longer codes than six digits
choices.why: There is no code for the person to type at all.

choices.text: Counting how many logins a user makes per day
choices.why: Rate limits are a separate measure.

choices.text: Matching the phone number to the SIM card
choices.why: That is a carrier's business, not this feature.

choices.text: Making TOTP codes longer and harder to guess
choices.why: It is for push approvals.

choices.text: Defeating MFA fatigue
choices.why: Right. Tapping yes to stop the noise no longer works.

prompt: Where should recovery codes be kept?

choices.text: Somewhere safe, away from the phone
choices.why: Right. They are a factor and are protected like one.

choices.text: They are not needed when MFA is on
choices.why: They are what you use when the phone is lost.

choices.text: In the email account they would help recover
choices.why: Then the recovery depends on the account being recovered.

choices.text: In a note on the same phone, so they are always at hand
choices.why: Lose the phone and the codes go with it.

prompt: A caller says they are a colleague who lost their phone and gives a number to call back. What does the lesson say to do?
hint: A channel the caller did not choose.

choices.text: Call back on the number they gave, to confirm it works
choices.why: That number is the caller's choice.

choices.text: Ask them their password to confirm their identity
choices.why: Nobody should ever be asked their password.

choices.text: Call the number in the staff records, or their manager
choices.why: Right. Verify through a channel the caller did not choose.

choices.text: Reset MFA at once, since the person sounds stressed
choices.why: Stress is part of a good pretext.

prompt: An account has a security key, and password reset works through an SMS code. How strong is the account?

choices.text: It depends only on the password
choices.why: The reset bypasses the password.

choices.text: As strong as the security key
choices.why: The attacker goes through the reset instead.

choices.text: Stronger than either, since there are two methods
choices.why: Two doors are weaker than one, not stronger.

choices.text: As strong as the SMS reset, the easier way in
choices.why: Right. An account is as strong as its easiest way in.

prompt: Which of these are true multi-factor logins? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: password and a TOTP code from an app
choices.why: Know and have.

choices.text: password and a security question
choices.why: Both are know.

choices.text: a security key and a fingerprint on it
choices.why: Have and are.

choices.text: password and the office network
choices.why: Location is a signal, not a factor.
